issues.legal_issue: A court answering a statutory tax reference must accept the facts stated by the tribunal unless the validity of those findings is properly before it.
material_facts: The tax tribunal found that the property owner supplied electricity, hot and cold water, lifts, scavenging, watch and ward facilities, and other amenities, using substantial permanent staff.
The question referred to the High Court proceeded on the facts found by the tribunal, and no question challenging the validity of those findings had been referred.
The High Court reappraised the evidence and rejected some of the tribunal’s factual findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limited jurisdiction of a reference by going behind the tribunal’s findings; it was required to answer the question on the facts stated by the tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 66 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, a High Court on a reference must take the facts as stated in the statement of the case unless the validity of the tribunal’s findings is properly in issue. The statement of the case binds the parties, as held in Kshetra Mohan Sannyasi Charan Sadhukhan v. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax, West Bengal.

predicates.income_tax_reference: The matter is a reference to a court for an opinion on a question of tax law.
predicates.tribunal_facts_stated: The tribunal has stated the facts on which the referred question proceeds.
predicates.tribunal_findings_not_challenged: No properly raised question asks the court to review the validity of the tribunal’s factual findings.

issues.definition: When a tax reference proceeds on facts stated by a tribunal and no challenge to those findings is before the court, the court must accept those facts.

issues.legal_issue: Income from continuously and systematically providing tenant services for profit is income from business activities.
material_facts: The property owner bought electricity in bulk, converted it for use in the premises, and supplied it to tenants.
The owner maintained facilities for supplying hot and cold water and provided lifts and other amenities.
The owner maintained a large permanent staff to provide these services, which were carried on continuously and in an organized manner with a view to earning profits.
The tribunal found that the service receipts were distinct from the rental receipts; that factual finding was not challenged in the reference.
issues.conclusion: On the facts found by the tribunal, the services were business activities and the income arising from them was assessable as business income under section 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, applies to income from business activities. Applying Salisbury House Estate Ltd. v. Fry, the Court treated the continuous, organized, profit-seeking provision of services as a business activity distinct on the facts from the ordinary letting of property. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay City v. National Storage Private Ltd. and Sultan Brothers Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay City-II were cited in argument but did not displace the result on the facts found.

rule.if: income_tax_classification_dispute and services_provided_continuously and services_organized_for_profit and services_distinct_from_rent_on_found_facts

predicates.income_tax_classification_dispute: The dispute concerns the tax classification of receipts earned by a property owner.
predicates.services_provided_continuously: The owner repeatedly provides services to occupants of the property.
predicates.services_organized_for_profit: The owner organizes the service activity and carries it on with a view to earning profits.
predicates.services_distinct_from_rent_on_found_fac: The fact finder treats the service activity and its receipts as distinct from the ordinary letting activity and rental receipts.

issues.definition: If a tax-classification dispute concerns services repeatedly and systematically provided for profit, and those services are distinct from letting on the facts found, the service receipts are business income.

issues.legal_issue: Factual findings in one tax assessment proceeding do not necessarily prevent their reconsideration in a later assessment proceeding.
material_facts: The Court did not examine whether the tribunal’s factual findings were correct; it accepted them because their validity was not in issue in the reference.
The dispute concerned tax assessment years, and the Court noted that the facts could still be considered in a future assessment.
issues.conclusion: The Court’s decision did not foreclose reconsideration of the factual findings in a future assessment; generally, res judicata does not apply to taxation proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The general rule is that res judicata does not apply to taxation proceedings. Because the Court had not reviewed the correctness of the tribunal’s findings, their correctness could remain open for consideration in a future assessment.

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the assessment of tax for an assessment period.
predicates.current_court_did_not_review_factual_cor: The court accepted the fact finder's findings without deciding whether they were factually correct.

issues.definition: When a court in a tax assessment proceeding has not reviewed the correctness of factual findings, a later assessment may reconsider those facts.
